Voiceless dental stop (p. 24).

Spelled ch: 'a voiceless retroflexed stop', 'sometimes called a voiceless retroflexed affricate'; Jensen 'will generally refer to it ... as a stop' (p. 24). Ross (1996) writes c (decision jensen1977-symbols).
Voiceless velar stop (p. 24).
Glottal stop, spelled q, also word-initially before a vowel (pp. 24-26).
Glottalized bilabial stop. Glottalized: the closed glottis is raised suddenly, so the release makes 'a popping sound' (pp. 27-28, 31): an ejective.
Glottalized dental stop. Glottalized: the closed glottis is raised suddenly, so the release makes 'a popping sound' (pp. 27-28, 31): an ejective.

Glottalized velar stop. Glottalized: the closed glottis is raised suddenly, so the release makes 'a popping sound' (pp. 27-28, 31): an ejective. There is no glottalized retroflex consonant (pp. 28-29).
Voiceless labiodental fricative (p. 29).
Spelled th: voiceless dental fricative (p. 29).
'A voiceless retroflexed fricative', made with the tip of the tongue 'somewhat behind the teeth' (p. 30).
Glottalized labiodental fricative; rare (pp. 30-31). Glottalized: the closed glottis is raised suddenly, so the release makes 'a popping sound' (pp. 27-28, 31): an ejective. Ross (1996) writes fˀ.
Glottalized dental fricative; rare (pp. 30-31). Glottalized: the closed glottis is raised suddenly, so the release makes 'a popping sound' (pp. 27-28, 31): an ejective.
Spelled b: 'a voiced bilabial obstruent', a stop after m and a fricative elsewhere (p. 33). Entered by its usual fricative value (decision jensen1977-symbols); Ross (1996) writes v.
Spelled d: 'a voiced dental obstruent', a stop after n (and for some speakers word-initially), a fricative elsewhere (p. 32).
Spelled g: 'a voiced velar obstruent', a stop after ng and a fricative elsewhere (p. 33).
Bilabial nasal (p. 34).
Dental nasal (p. 34). There is no retroflex nasal.
Velar nasal (p. 34).

Glottalized bilabial nasal; common, but rare word-finally (p. 35). A plain sonorant 'interrupted by a glottal stop': the glottal stop comes at the beginning word-initially, at the end word-finally and in the middle word-medially (pp. 34-37).

Glottalized dental nasal (p. 35). A plain sonorant 'interrupted by a glottal stop': the glottal stop comes at the beginning word-initially, at the end word-finally and in the middle word-medially (pp. 34-37).

Glottalized velar nasal, 'extremely rare', in 'three or four words' (p. 35). A plain sonorant 'interrupted by a glottal stop': the glottal stop comes at the beginning word-initially, at the end word-finally and in the middle word-medially (pp. 34-37).
Dental lateral (p. 36).
'A voiced retroflexed trill': the tongue, 'in a retroflexed position', 'lightly taps the roof of the mouth a few times' (p. 36).

Glottalized lateral; there is no glottalized r (pp. 36-37). A plain sonorant 'interrupted by a glottal stop': the glottal stop comes at the beginning word-initially, at the end word-finally and in the middle word-medially (pp. 34-37).
Semivowel (p. 37).
Semivowel, spelled y (p. 37).
Glottalized semivowel, only syllable-finally, ending in a glottal stop; some speakers have q instead (pp. 37-38).
Glottalized semivowel, only syllable-finally, ending in a glottal stop (pp. 37-38).
Voiceless glottal fricative, 'not a native Yapese sound': only in a few loans (haang 'seal', kaahool 'box'), never word-finally (p. 30).
'A voiced retroflexed obstruent' in 'a very few borrowed words' (juboeng 'trousers'): a fricative, a stop after n (p. 33).
